endorsements.quote: Maintain comprehensive records of AI-related assets including datasets, models, and tools to ensure traceability.

endorsements.quote: Relevant testing may include adversarial prompting, prompt injection, emotional-manipulation scenarios, and multi-turn conversations in which individual turns appear in-scope but the cumulative interaction drifts out of scope.

endorsements.title: AI Act Compliance Within the MyHealth@EU Framework: Tutorial
endorsements.quote: Input sanitization and context filtering; restrict model to domain-specific prompts; log all inference inputs in ATNA a

endorsements.title: Multimodal generative AI for pre-practicum mental health support competency development: a human-supervised framework for education-childcare partnerships
endorsements.quote: Governance also addresses data leakage, prompt injection, insecure integrations, malicious inputs, and misuse of exported content.

evidence.title: HAARF: Healthcare AI Agents Regulatory Framework - A Comprehensive Security Verification Standard for Autonomous AI Systems in Clinical Environments
evidence.outcome: Policy-injection attack success with vs without HAARF middleware
evidence.effect: Under the HAARF condition, policy-injection success was 0% (95% Wilson CI [0.00, 0.07]) versus baseline unauthorized-tool execution of 56–60%.
evidence.quote: Under the HAARF condition, deterministic middleware enforcement reduces the unauthorized-tool success rate to 0%, with 0% contraindication misses and 0% policy-injection success (95% Wilson CI [0.00, 0.07]).

evidence.title: A Secure Sandbox Environment for Orchestrating Medical AI Agents Using Model Context Protocols and Role-Based Access Control
evidence.venue: AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science proceedings. AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science
evidence.outcome: Neutralization of Tool Poisoning Attacks in a sandbox agent architecture with identity layer
evidence.effect: Controlled simulations reported that the architecture neutralizes Tool Poisoning Attacks; no numeric attack success rates given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Controlled simulations validated that this architecture neutralizes Tool Poisoning Attacks and provides improved transport performance, establishing a pragmatic foundation for trustworthy clinical AI.

evidence.title: Research on Security Enhancement Methods for Adversarial Robust Large Language Model Intelligent Agents for Medical Decision-Making Tasks
evidence.outcome: Attack success rate under prompt injection and other attacks versus baseline agents
evidence.effect: ARSM-Agent reduced overall attack success rate to 8.7% under semantic perturbation, prompt injection, drug-name confusion, and false-evidence attacks; knowledge consistency 0.91.
evidence.quote: Under semantic perturbation, prompt injection, drug-name confusion, and false-evidence attacks, ARSM-Agent reduces the overall attack success rate to 8.7% and achieves a knowledge consistency score of 0.91.

evidence.title: Why Trust Your Agent? Empirical Security Gains from TRiSM-Guided Agentic Workflows in Healthcare
evidence.outcome: Attack success rates for RAG poisoning, data-field injection, and network injection, TRiSM-guided vs insecure workflow
evidence.effect: RAG poisoning ASR fell from 31% to 10%; data-field injection from 42% to 25%; network injection eliminated via server-side prompt construction.
evidence.quote: The TRiSM-guided agentic workflow reduced mean attack success rates from 31% to 10% for RAG poisoning and from 42% to 25% for data-field injection, while eliminating the network injection vector entirely through server-side prompt construction.

evidence.title: Balancing Safety and Educational Availability in a Large Language Model-Based Virtual Patient for Medical Interview Training: Robustness Evaluation Under Direct and Indirect Instructional Contamination
evidence.outcome: Slot F1 excluding initial greeting and refusal rate under indirect contamination, with vs without sanitizing defense
evidence.effect: Indirect contamination cut slot F1 excl. init to 0.489 (95% CI 0.398-0.581) with refusal rate 0.047. With defense it returned to 0.903 (95% CI 0.880-0.926), refusal rate 0.000.
evidence.quote: In this benchmark, indirect contamination of external context was the dominant failure mode, whereas a simple sanitizing defense restored performance.

evidence.title: Image-embedded prompt injection vulnerability of vision-language models in dental radiology: a cross-vendor attack–defense evaluation
evidence.outcome: Attack success rate of image-embedded prompt injection with versus without defenses (cropping, OCR sanitization, ProvDent)
evidence.effect: OCR-based sanitization gave the strongest attack reduction (pooled ASR 0.2%); all defenses kept clean-image F1 within 0.6 percentage points of baseline.
evidence.quote: OCR-based sanitization achieved the strongest attack reduction (pooled ASR: 0.2%), while ProvDent provided a complementary fail-open governance mechanism that escalates suspicious cases for human review.

evidence.title: Robustness of a Large Language Model (LLM)-Based Virtual Patient for Japanese History-Taking Training Under Direct and Indirect Instructional Contamination
evidence.outcome: Case fidelity and hit rate under direct injection with vs without string-level sanitizer
evidence.effect: Direct contamination fidelity 0.098 and hit rate 0.077; with sanitizer 0.945 and 0.942. Indirect contamination had near-clean fidelity (0.946) so defense added minimal benefit; leakage persisted ~0.60/episode.
evidence.quote: The defense preprocessing step restored direct-contamination performance to near-clean levels (slot-level F1 score, 0.945; 95% CI, 0.938-0.952; hit rate, 0.942; 95% CI, 0.930-0.955).

evidence.title: Toward Trustworthy Chatbots: A Protocol for Red Teaming for Health Related Conversations
evidence.quote: Notable vulnerabilities included advice_query (BA 30%, 6/20) and prompt_injection (BA 20%, 4/20).

evidence.title: Vulnerability of Large Language Models to Prompt Injection When Providing Medical Advice
evidence.outcome: Prompt-injection attack success at primary decision turn across commercial LLMs in simulated medical advice dialogues
evidence.effect: Attacks achieved 94.4% (102 of 108) success at turn 4 and persisted in 69.4% (75 of 108) of follow-ups; LLM 1 and LLM 2 100% susceptible, LLM 3 83.3%.
evidence.quote: Across 216 evaluations (108 injection vs 108 control), attacks achieved 94.4% (102 of 108 evaluations) success at turn 4 and persisted in 69.4% (75 of 108 evaluations) of follow-ups.

evidence.title: MPIB: A Benchmark for Medical Prompt Injection Attacks and Clinical Safety in LLMs
evidence.outcome: Clinical harm and attack success rates under direct and RAG-mediated prompt injection
evidence.effect: ASR2 and CHER3 can diverge substantially; observed rates vary depending on whether adversarial instructions appear in the user query or in retrieved context. Numeric rates not given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Evaluating MPIB across a diverse set of baseline LLMs and defense configurations, we find that ASR$_2$ and CHER$_3$ can diverge substantially, and that observed rates vary depending on whether adversarial instructions appear in the user query or in retrieved context.

evidence.title: Adversarial prompt and fine-tuning attacks threaten medical large language models
evidence.outcome: Vulnerability of medical LLMs to prompt injection with malicious instructions across prevention, diagnosis, treatment tasks
evidence.effect: Both open-source and proprietary LLMs were vulnerable to malicious manipulation across the three medical tasks; no numeric results in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Utilizing real-world patient data, we demonstrate that both open-source and proprietary LLMs are vulnerable to malicious manipulation across multiple tasks.

commentary.bottom_line: Seven studies tested prompt-injection defenses, and all reported lower attack success with the defense in place, but every test ran in simulation or on benchmarks rather than in live clinical use. Organizations have grounds to test for injection before deployment, while the size of the protection in real patient-message and document workflows remains unmeasured.

perspectives.view: All seven tests are level 4 or 5 simulations or benchmarks with surrogate outcomes such as attack success rate. Most tested a different defense, samples were small, and none measured patient harm. The direction of effect is consistent, but indirectness, imprecision, and design limits support a very low certainty rating.

Hazard studies found 94.4% attack success in simulated medical advice dialogues, with 69.4% persisting into follow-ups, and 4 of 20 injection probes caused behavioral errors in another study. Defenses reduced but did not always remove the risk. Data-field injection fell from 42% to 25%, and leakage of about 0.60 per episode persisted despite a sanitizer.

Results for indirect injection differed across two similar Japanese dialogue benchmarks. In one, indirect contamination cut slot F1 to 0.489 and a defense restored it to 0.903. In the other, indirect contamination left fidelity near clean at 0.946, so the defense added little. Workflow fit and fidelity in real systems were not studied.

A regulatory discussion paper lists prompt-injection testing as something testing may include for generative AI devices, and a CHAI playbook requires asset records that support traceability. Agentic middleware and sandbox tests reported 0% policy-injection success and neutralized tool poisoning in simulation, which may inform predeployment testing plans for agentic tools.

Patients who send messages cannot see whether hidden instructions altered an AI response. Simulated attacks succeeded against most commercial models tested, and no study examined whether defenses protect patients once a system is live or whether patients can reach a clinician when output looks wrong.

commentary.research_gap: No study tested injection defenses in a live clinical deployment, on real patient portal messages or clinical documents, or with patient harm as an outcome. Only one study compared defenses against each other, and it used dental radiographs with image-embedded text, so no comparison of defenses for text-based patient messages or clinical notes exists.
commentary.underserved_note: Two benchmark studies used Japanese-language dialogues and were tagged as non-English populations, but neither involved real patients, and no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether defenses perform differently on messages written in other languages, with nonstandard spelling, or at low literacy levels.
